inline.s: Instructions for the Layman Lianxi

When a deluded thought arises, still it on the spot; / let no single thought be left to hang upon the heart. / To forget all contrivance is the true Land of Peace — / why seek the Pure Land outside, somewhere apart?
Inscribed at the Ink-Light Pavilion Where Master Da Copied the Sutras

They tell how a lotus blooms beneath his brush; / the ink’s own light still shines in the empty brightness. / Idly I ask the master within the flower — / my ears are filled with autumn waves preaching the Dharma.
Instructions for the Student Cao Xiqing

A true man’s resolve is not of the common kind: / thigh stabbed, hair bound to the beam, all hardship tasted. / Only let the six senses stay undefiled, / and light will of itself rise in the ground of mind.
Inscribed on a Wall While Roaming Mount Fu, Having Heard the Chan Monk Zhideng Recite the Lotus Sutra Below Miaogao Peak
A lotus on the water, the sutra on his tongue; / one hut is locked deep in ten thousand green peaks. / Pine winds by day and night are preaching still — / a pity that the people cannot hear.
Instructions for the Novice Monk Zhensi

Birth and death, impermanence, rest on a single breath; / better to set your heart’s will on the green hills. / Only do no karma of the dusty world, / and you win a whole life’s leisure beyond all things.
On Mount Kuang, Pleased by the Visit of Chen Chishi, Grand Councillor

Ten thousand folds of green hills, one single mind; / wherever the eye falls, cloud-forest everywhere. / No need to ask again the meaning of the West’s coming — / water-birds now and then proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
Instructions for the Elder Xiu Liuyi, Who Kept Retreat at Golden Wheel Peak

When you sit alone atop a peak ten thousand fathoms high, / to drop both body and mind is to raise the whole affair. / The silver mountain, the iron wall, must be bored through: / utterly clear throughout — yet no knowing may enter there.
Seeing Off Chief Seat Wuxin Rong, Returning to Jingkou

In the empty hills I meant to spend my last years with you; / why should you sail eastward on the Dharma boat? / Wait until the lone moon rises over the sea-gate, / then round off one huatou for this old monk.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Daben

Pierce through the dusty world and the mind of ten thousand kalpas; / come home into the deep white clouds. / Below Golden Wheel Peak the pine billows race — / day by day hear the wondrous Dharma of the unborn.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Benhuai

Your body and mind have long dwelt in the white clouds; / why let conditions blow you about like tumbling weeds? / Gather yourself home and lay everything down; / lie high in the ten thousand hills, with the sun red overhead.
Instructions for the Attendant Xingsu

Cast off body and mind and bow to the Dharma King; / no need to ask the road ahead, to stay or go. / Only know the face you had before your mother bore you, / and grasses, trees, and thickets all give forth light.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Dunli on His Pilgrimage to Mount Wutai
One staff in hand, one gourd slung along; / do not shrink from ten thousand miles of pilgrimage. / If you meet Mañjuśrī on the day of the feast, / take care no bucket of foul water douse your head.
Instructions for the Two Chan Monks Jizhi and Huilin
A student need not strive and seek in pain; / when delusions melt away, you are free. / Just throw on your robe and watch in idleness — / whose stream is it that follows thought on thought?

The empty hills are still, all conditions cut; / I do not learn the five-flavored Chan of other places. / One who inquires need not seek what goes upward; / simply let go, and all is natural as it is.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Hengyi

This matter has never been sought outside; / seeing, hearing, knowing have their ground. / Know only that in daily use it shows at every turn; / do not fall into the second rank of following conditions.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Kewen

Flowers in the sky rise and vanish without a cause; / yet how each one stares with a film-shrouded eye. / Trust that in the clear sky it is nowhere to be found: / a true man must never be fooled by it.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Juhe

Sitting through a thousand peaks, I do not ask about Chan; / incense in the censer and sutra scrolls are my livelihood. / If beyond this there is nothing else to do, / then this dusty world is the heaven of Extreme Bliss.
Instructions Given When Chief Seat Ruoxing Jiong Came from Afar to Inquire

In the sea of suffering we followed one another twenty years; / once more from Mount Lu you come to bow to dry-bones Chan. / Look at me and ask nothing of the years that remain: / the Five Elders’ cloud-haze is there before our eyes.
A Verse for the Chan Monk Nianyun on His Sixtieth Birthday, He Having Served as Host at Wujiang by His Patriarch’s Command

In the dust of the world the road of awakening opens a cloud-hall; / body and mind spread out, filling the ten directions. / One patch of the Patriarch’s ever-abiding ground — / may it serve as ford and bridge through endless kalpas.
Instructions for Meizi

The burning house blazes; it is not easily cooled. / How pitiable that the six senses are scorched away. / But if a single thought can be cold as ice, / that is the first stage of passing beyond the ordinary.
Seeing Off Dharma Master Mei, Who Goes to Lecture at Weiyang

By chance you ride a single reed and cut across the river; / the Dharma drum thunders at the farther shore. / Countless beings wake from the great dream — / and you return, your bright mark never once withdrawn.
Instructions for the Layman Zheng Baisheng

When this one piece of body and mind is laid down, / let it be within and without like crystal. / There is no place in it for the least dust to cling; / in daily use, each turn is known to oneself alone.
Instructions for the Elder Fuwu Ang, Hall Master of Caoxi

I often think of the long-haired monk of Xinzhou; / he knew not a single word — what power was his? / A load of firewood on his shoulder, a stone at his waist, / and he won the endless lamp that came from the West.
The place of practice need not be sought elsewhere; / it lies in a single thought of the one before you. / If self-nature can appear in full, / why fear the Dharma-sea will not flow across the world?
Instructions for the Chan Monk Jiankong

To leave the dust, my first intent was the mountain woods; / at forty still unheard of, I am shamed before this mind. / Now I rejoice the silken thread at my heel is broken; / deep in ten thousand peaks, deeper still is best.
Instructions for a Chan Monk on His Pilgrimage to Mount Emei
Take the boundless Dharmadhātu as your body; / wherever you meet it, the intimacy is closest. / But if you go to the summit of Mount Emei, / cloud and glow fill the eyes and bewilder you more.

Westward I gaze on Emei, its snow like silver; / Samantabhadra sits upright in a single mote of dust. / The boundless ocean of lands is held within — / appearing as conditions call, the body that joys to be seen.
Instructions for Master Ye on the Casting of a Bell

Heaven and earth the furnace, all things the bronze; / melted into many openings, it roars in the long wind. / One note rings through the three-thousandfold world / and wakes the world from its great dream.
Instructions for the Student Li

In this floating world the light of day is bitterly brief. / What of the matter beneath your own feet — how goes it? / If in this life you do not seek a place of rest, / you will drift with conditions into the river of love.
Instructions for the Ascetic Pu, Who Begs for His Food

The market far, the hills deep, the begging road is long; / you carry only one bowl along the endless way. / Do not weary of the windings of the road: / remember Huangmei, and the stone that dragged at his waist.
Instructions for Dharma Master Wuyin

Once you circled the King of Emptiness by the flower throne; / from letters and words the fragrance of prajñā rose. / Now on a single hair you behold the ocean of lands: / meeting others, there is no need of fine deliberation.
Instructions for the Old Monk Huanzong, Who Printed the Avataṃsaka Sutra

Split a mote of dust and the great sutra comes forth; / the Dharma-gates are a net of pearls, each shaping the next. / Clearly it holds up the Lotus Treasury whole — / wherever it touches, it wakes the dreaming eye.
Presented to the Old Monk Xiangshan, Master of Geomancy

Mountains and rivers of the great earth are empty in his eye; / his one staff is alive as a dragon. / Clearly he points out the road of the unborn, / straight through to the one stream that came from the West.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Tiju
Zhaozhou’s “no” is the pass of birth and death; / the iron wall and silver mountain, seen with cold eyes. / Only see through it before your birth, / and no tongue will ever deceive you.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Yue, Who Gives Tea at the Qingliang Hut

With a willow spray he sprinkles sweet dew on the scorched and withered; / one drop touches, and fevered anguish revives. / Pointing straight at the true meaning of the West’s coming — / when we meet, he only asks: have you taken tea?
Sent to Wuyi Yuanlai of Mount Bo

Our hearts’ accord is not parted by a hairtip; / across a thousand miles of cloud-hills we meet face to face. / Most intimate of all when I long for you: / deep in the night, the bright moon chills the one it shines on.
Instructions for the Elder of Shouchang

Tiles and rubble turn into a great place of practice; / let not the Patriarch’s field lie fallow. / Remember the words: braving rain and piercing cold — / a grain of rice, a stalk of firewood can break the heart.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Qu Ranmi of Shouchang
The lion in his pit has long been trained in play; / his turning and leaping are not easy to know. / Do not let the wild fox’s tracks draw near; / the bared fangs — remember them at the moment.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Wanshi

Bury the body where no wind blows from any of the eight sides; / only when the thieving mind is dead does the work show. / Put your strength on the place before your birth, / and you will know the sun reddening beneath the sea.
Instructions for the Old Monk Bixia

You have traveled every other land and long since come home; / the temple, your native hills, opens where you sit. / A monk who enters the gate has nothing else to do: / to drink tea and wash the bowl is wonderful enough.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Xuanshu
The matter beneath your own feet must be clear; / raise one thought alone and do not count the miles. / Where delusive feeling is wholly spent, / the waters of mind will of themselves run clear.
Instructions for the Old Monk Guizong of Qiyang

Whatever meets the eye is plainly prajñā’s light; / the six gates ever shine, never concealed. / If in a single thought sense and object are cut off, / then in daily use, sitting still, you are in the great place of practice.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Huijing
The light seen by the mind is not in the senses; / darkness has never been able to dim it. / The three-thousandfold world is like a fruit in the palm — / Aniruddha himself entered by this gate.
Instructions for the Elder Liuru Kun, Who Kept Retreat

Gather in body and mind and shut the gate fast; / amid the dust it is no different from the deep hills. / Cast away all delusive thoughts, / and from now on seek diligently the leisure beyond the world.
Instructions for the Attendant Jieshen Jun

I recall how once, bottle in hand and following a staff, / time and again for the Dharma I came to Caoxi. / Now you come straight into the thousand peaks / and ask before the hall to be pointed past delusion.
Instructions for Youming Liaozhong on His Pilgrimage to Wuru

In years past, having finished your pilgrimage, you bowed at Qingliang; / one glimpse of Mañjuśrī and you returned home. / Not knowing how many are in the three-three assembly, / you come again to ask that it be expounded.
Instructions Given When Zheng Baisheng Came Again to Consult Me at Wuru

Yesterday you came past Mount Kuang to ask the Dharma; / did you understand the one phrase raised in full? / Only do not forget the road by which you go home, / and you will of yourself pass beyond the paths of sage and ordinary being.
Sent in Reply on Hearing That Shen Langqian Had Entered Retreat in the City
One room amid the market, open as space; / ordinary and sage mingle and fall within it. / Only the host is ever still and silent, / sitting through the ten directions where no wind blows.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Huikong of Guanyin Mountain in Danyang

Outside the Jetavana gate lies the ford of delusion; / wind and waves come and go, and passing travelers are many. / Hold high the lamp of wisdom, never dimmed: / it must shine right through a single mote of dust.
Instructions for the Chan Monk Andu

The sea of illusion is boundless, its waves not yet stilled; / trust wholly the oar of wisdom to steer the boat of compassion. / Midstream, hoist the light sail high and go, / straight on to the farther shore of bodhi.
Sent to Jin Zhendu
When we sat together at Jetavana at the meal, / since we parted I often recall your good contemplation. / Your Dharma bond must be like Vimalakīrti’s: / who lately has talked with you of non-duality?
Sent to the Chan Monk Yuguang of Mount Putuo

Long have you sat cross-legged below White Flower Mountain; / in the light of water and moon, one thought stands alone. / Even should you sit through all the ten directions, / seas dry and rocks rot — it is as though nothing were.
In Reply to Dharma Master Xinguang

In the empty hills one room is sealed by white clouds; / a bird’s path, subtle and fine, leads into ten thousand folds. / Were it not a road running straight beyond the heavens, / how would you know each step erases all trace?
Instructions for the Attendant Shenguang, Who Goes Home to Visit His Parents

Twenty years have passed since you left your kind mother; / you must clarify the state before your parents were born. / And now again you dream of going home: / this time you should cut the bonds of love.
Instructions for the Layman Yao Xingyang

Your mind is in the dust, yet you vow to leave the dust; / you must simply not be blind to the original person. / Ever and again recall where you take refuge: / among the eight-jewel flowers a latter body waits.
Instructions for the Old Monk Liaoci on the Increase of His Monastic Years

In this turbid world of floating life, do not ask the years; / the dharmakāya is not moved by the three times. / Only let one thought of constant light appear, / and the Lotus Treasury’s adornment is before your eyes.
Instructions for the Attendant Who Guards the Retreat Gate

Lifting the tea, offering water, you must truly know; / in movement and stillness, in turning about, see who it is. / You must look to where the three calls come before your eyes; / do not let those two eyebrows be wasted.
The rhinoceros fan is whole in bone and hide; / called for in haste, it cannot be picked up. / One word stings like three strokes of the rod — / how few can catch the fist beneath the ribs?
Instructions for the Chan Monk Benyuan of Yangshan in Xin’an

Cutting off love, know it is the cause of leaving the world; / would you let a speck of dust settle on the ground of mind? / Each thought must turn the light back and shine within; / be not blind to your own pure dharmakāya.

One thought of perfect clarity, hidden nowhere; / wherever it meets conditions, all is the light of stillness. / Pick up one mote of dust and the Dharmadhātu is held there — / where else would you look for the Western Land?
Sent to the Venerable Chongxu of Jiming Temple

Lake light and mountain colors shine before your bed; / the towers seem lotuses rising from the water. / Afar I recall where my old friend takes his joy: / sitting in Chan at white noon among the flowers.
Sent to the Venerable Liaoxin of Mount Huangbo

Chan from Huangbo is hardest to inquire into; / no sooner touched by words than it falls to second and third. / Only the wind and light are held up in one palm; / and to this day the hills and waters murmur on.
Sent to the Master of Fan Mountain
